title: NAT & Firewalls
summary: IPv4 addresses ran out decades ago. NAT lets thousands of devices share one public IP — and firewalls decide which traffic is allowed through.

blocks.markdown:
**NAT (Network Address Translation)** rewrites IP addresses in packet headers, letting many devices share one public IP. **Firewalls** inspect packets and decide what traffic is allowed.

- NAT solves IPv4 exhaustion and hides internal address structure.
- Firewalls enforce policy at the network edge.
- Both live in the same router/appliance in most home and office networks.
- See [ipv4-addressing](ipv4-addressing) for why the address space is limited.

IPv4 has ~4.3 billion addresses — exhausted globally by 2011. NAT is the workaround.

- **Private address ranges** (e.g. 192.168.x.x, 10.x.x.x) are not routable on the public internet.
- A NAT device sits at the boundary and rewrites source addresses outbound, so internal hosts appear as one public IP.
- Side effect: internal topology is hidden from the outside — a mild form of obscurity.
- Does NOT replace [ipv6](ipv6), which is the permanent fix.

blocks.subTitle: Static NAT
blocks.markdown:
**Static NAT** maps one private IP to one fixed public IP — a permanent, one-to-one assignment.

- The mapping never changes; inbound connections can reach the internal host reliably.
- Used for servers (web, mail) that must be reachable from outside.
- Requires one public IP per internal host — expensive; doesn't save addresses.

blocks.subTitle: Dynamic NAT
blocks.markdown:
**Dynamic NAT** maps private IPs to a **pool** of public IPs, assigned on demand.

- The router picks a free public IP from the pool when an internal host connects out.
- When the session ends the public IP returns to the pool.
- Still one-to-one at any moment — if the pool is full, new connections are blocked.
- Rarely used; PAT (below) is almost always chosen instead.

blocks.subTitle: PAT — the common one
blocks.markdown:
**PAT (Port Address Translation)**, also called **NAT overload**, maps many private IPs to a single public IP using different **source port numbers** to tell sessions apart.

- 192.168.1.10:5001 → 203.0.113.1:40001
- 192.168.1.11:5001 → 203.0.113.1:40002
- Thousands of hosts share one public IP simultaneously.
- This is what every home router does. The NAT table tracks (private IP, private port) ↔ (public IP, public port).

- On the way **out**: router rewrites source IP+port → public IP+unique port, saves mapping.
- On the way **back**: router looks up the port, rewrites destination back to the original private host.

**Port forwarding** is a static NAT rule that lets inbound traffic reach a specific internal host.

- Rule: traffic arriving on public port 8080 → forward to 192.168.1.50:80.
- Needed because PAT blocks unsolicited inbound connections by default.
- Used for home servers, gaming, remote desktop.
- Creates a permanent hole in the NAT table — only punch through what you need.

blocks.subTitle: What a firewall is
blocks.markdown:
A **firewall** is a device (or software) that inspects network traffic and allows or blocks it based on rules.

- Sits between a trusted network (internal) and an untrusted one (internet).
- Rules match on fields like source IP, destination IP, port, and protocol.
- **Default deny**: block everything, then whitelist what's allowed — the safe baseline.
- See [network-security-attacks](network-security-attacks) for what firewalls defend against.

blocks.subTitle: Stateless vs stateful
blocks.markdown:
The key distinction in firewall design.

| | Stateless (packet filter) | Stateful |
|---|---|---|
| Inspects | Each packet alone | Packet + connection state |
| Tracks sessions | No | Yes — connection table |
| Speed | Faster, simpler | Slightly more overhead |
| Attack surface | Spoofed packets can slip through | Rejects out-of-state packets |

**Stateful** is the modern default. It knows a reply packet belongs to an established session, so it doesn't need a separate rule to allow it.

blocks.subTitle: ACLs — access control lists
blocks.markdown:
**ACLs (Access Control Lists)** are the ordered rule sets that define what a firewall permits.

- Each rule: match (source IP, dest IP, port, protocol) → action (permit/deny).
- Rules evaluated **top to bottom**; first match wins.
- An implicit **deny all** at the bottom drops unmatched traffic.
- Wrong rule order is a common misconfiguration — a broad permit before a narrow deny swallows the deny.

blocks.subTitle: L3/L4 vs application firewalls
blocks.markdown:
Traditional firewalls operate at **L3 (IP) and L4 (TCP/UDP)** — they see addresses and ports, not payload content.

- Can block or allow a connection to port 443, but can't inspect what's inside the HTTPS stream.
- **Application firewalls** (L7) decode the protocol — HTTP headers, SQL queries, cookies.
- **WAF (Web Application Firewall)** is the common L7 type: blocks SQLi, XSS, and other web attacks by inspecting HTTP payloads.
- WAFs terminate TLS so they can read the plaintext request. See [tls-ssl](tls-ssl).

Common mistakes:

- **"NAT is a firewall."** No — NAT rewrites addresses; it doesn't enforce policy. A router doing NAT with no firewall rules passes all outbound traffic freely.
- **"NAT fixes IPv4 exhaustion."** It delays it; IPv6 is the real fix.
- **"Stateless and stateful are equivalent."** Stateless can be fooled by spoofed ACK packets that look like replies to non-existent sessions.
- **"Port forwarding is safe if the port is obscure."** Security by obscurity fails; open ports get scanned regardless.

blocks.subTitle: What is NAT and why is it used?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is NAT and why is it used?**

NAT (Network Address Translation) rewrites source IP addresses in packet headers so many private hosts can share a single public IP. It exists because IPv4's ~4.3 billion addresses are exhausted — private ranges (10.x, 192.168.x) are not routable, so the NAT device translates them at the boundary. Side benefit: hides internal topology.

blocks.subTitle: PAT vs static NAT
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between static NAT and PAT?**

Static NAT = one private IP ↔ one public IP, permanent mapping. PAT (NAT overload) = many private IPs share one public IP, distinguished by unique source port numbers. PAT is what home routers use; static NAT is for internal servers that must accept inbound connections.

blocks.subTitle: Stateless vs stateful firewall
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Stateless vs stateful firewall — what's the difference?**

A stateless (packet filter) firewall evaluates each packet in isolation against ACL rules. A stateful firewall tracks connection state — it knows which sessions are established and can automatically allow reply traffic without explicit rules. Stateful is stronger because it rejects out-of-state packets (e.g. a spoofed TCP ACK with no matching SYN).

**Q: What is port forwarding?**

A static NAT rule that directs inbound traffic on a specific public port to a fixed internal host:port. Needed because PAT blocks unsolicited inbound by default.
